newsitem.title: INDIA: Sikh party takes office in India's Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Sikh party takes office in India's Punjab.

text.p: A Sikh party took power in India's farming state of Punjab on Wednesday days after it won a sweeping victory in local elections on a pledge of peace and development.

Some 30,000 cheering supporters of the Akali Dal, the Sikhs' main party, and the rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) thronged a sports stadium in the state capital of Chandigarh as Prakash Singh Badal was sworn in as chief minister.
It was a major comeback for the 69-year-old Badal, who has governed the state twice before, in 1970 and 1977, and marked a humiliating rout for the once-monolithic Congress party.
Underlining the newly-forged Sikh-Hindu alliance, two of Badal's nine cabinet ministers were Hindu leaders of the BJP.
Badal took the oath amid shouts of "Long live Hindu-Sikh unity" and "Long live the unity of Punjab".
The unity pledge was significant in a region torn by nearly two decades of Sikh separatist violence.
Nearly 20,000 people are estimated to have died in a bloody Sikh militant push for a homeland they called Khalistan.

The revolt was put down by thousands of troops, but the Akali Dal boycotted state elections in 1992 that ended five years of direct rule by the federal government and were held under the shadow of violence.
"We will give the people of Punjab an honest and transparent government," Badal told Reuters on Tuesday. "We want the people of Punjab to rejoice in this historic victory."
Political analysts were cautious about the future of the new Punjab administration.

"They are not in a position to say anything like the Pope of Christendom who had declared: 'We have got the papacy; let us enjoy it'," columnist S.S. Dhanoa wrote in Punjab's main English newspaper the Tribune.
"The Akalis and the BJP have yet to prove that they can remain united and provide clean and effective governance to the trouble-torn Punjab," Dhanoa said.
The Akali Dal and the BJP together won a four-fifths majority in last Friday's polls for the 117-member state legislature.
"This marks the inauguration of a new era in Punjab," former Akali interior minister Kanwaljit Singh told Reuters after he took the oath of office.
"We are no longer concerned only with the Sikhs of Punjab, we have changed the focus to carry all the Punjabis with us."
The Congress party, which won the 1992 elections with 87 seats, won only 14 seats in the Friday election. The Akali Dal won 74 seats and the BJP won 18.
An independent survey showed Congress garnered only 27 percent of votes in Punjab. Its previous low was in 1980 when it won 33 percent.
Sikhs form the majority in Punjab, but constitute only two percent of India's population of 936 million. Hindus comprise 82 percent.
